transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, doctor. Thanks for seeing me. Um, I'm here because flying has started to feel way scarier than it really should. Just the idea of getting on a plane makes me picture that turbulence from my honeymoon flight all over again. I mean, logically I know people fly safely every single day, but I just can't seem to shake that fear.

When you think about that turbulent flight from your honeymoon, do you find yourself having unwanted memories or flashbacks of it at times when you're not planning to fly—like during your daily activities?

No, not really. I don't get flashbacks or anything like that. It's really just... if I have to actually fly or think about booking a trip. When I'm just going about my normal day, I don't think about it at all.
Have you been avoiding booking flights or turning down opportunities to travel by plane because of this fear?

Yeah, I have. I mean, I've been choosing to take really long drives instead, or I'll just turn down work trainings so I don't have to fly. And if I absolutely have to even talk about a trip, I need my husband sitting right there with me just to get through it without backing out.

latest_inference.note: Patient denies intrusive flashbacks or unwanted memories outside of flight-related triggers, ruling out F40.02 (PTSD). Symptoms are specific to flying situation with clear avoidance and safety-seeking behavior, consistent with specific phobia of flying (F40.01).

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent, intense fear of flying triggered by a specific traumatic event (turbulent flight during honeymoon). She demonstrates marked avoidance behaviors (refusing flights, taking long drives, declining work opportunities) and requires reassurance/support from her husband to discuss flying. While she experienced a traumatic stressor, she denies intrusive recollections, flashbacks, or hyperarousal symptoms outside of flight-related situations, which are core features of PTSD. The clinical picture is most consistent with specific phobia (F40.01 - fear of flying/acrophobia) rather than post-traumatic stress disorder, as the fear is circumscribed to the flying situation itself and does not meet the broader criteria for PTSD.
